cases.title: Evaluate a dependency
cases.text: Before adopting a new open source library, check its actual size, not just file count. A 50-file repo might be 20k lines of dense C++ or 500 lines of glue code. SLOC gives you the real picture before you commit to a dependency.

cases.title: Estimate project scope
cases.text: Clients and stakeholders ask how big a codebase is. SLOC gives you a solid number before a review or audit: 12k lines across 8 languages, 89% code, 4% comments.

cases.title: Compare forks or alternatives
cases.text: Paste two repos and compare language breakdowns side by side. See how much a fork diverged, or how different two implementations of the same spec really are.

steps.title: Resolve
steps.text: OctoCounts validates the public GitHub URL and resolves the requested branch, tag, or commit SHA to a pinned commit hash via the GitHub API. Pinning to a commit means the analysis is deterministic: the same URL and ref always produce the same count, and the cache key is stable regardless of branch movement.

steps.title: Count
steps.text: The Rust backend downloads a compressed archive, not a full git clone. It skips generated folders like node_modules, vendor, and .git, then tokei counts every source file in a background worker queue.

steps.title: Cache
steps.text: Reports are stored by owner, repo, commit SHA, and tokei version. When you re-analyze the same commit, the cache is hit immediately, with no re-download and no re-count. Re-run forces a fresh analysis and updates the cache. The browser extension also caches results locally for instant offline viewing.

faq.question: What is an OctoCounts badge?
faq.answer: A small live image you embed in a README that shows repository SLOC stats and links to the permanent OctoCounts report page.

faq.question: How do I add a badge to my README?
faq.answer: Pick a badge type above, copy the Markdown snippet, and paste it into your README.md where you want the badge to appear.

faq.question: Will the badge slow down my README?
faq.answer: No. Badges are lightweight SVG images served by the OctoCounts badge API and are cached by CDN.

faq.question: Can I show a single language instead of the whole repo?
faq.answer: Yes. Select 'Single language' in the badge builder and enter the language name, for example Rust or TypeScript.

faq.question: Does the badge update automatically?
faq.answer: The badge reflects the latest cached report for the requested ref. Re-analyze the repository or visit its OctoCounts report to refresh the cache.

extensionLanding.heroTitle: See GitHub code statistics in your browser
extensionLanding.heroIntro: OctoCounts is a free browser extension that adds a SLOC (source lines of code) card to public GitHub repository pages. The card shows the repository's total line count at a glance; clicking it opens a full panel with files, code lines, comment lines, blank lines, and a per-language breakdown — the same counts the OctoCounts web app produces with tokei, pinned to an exact commit.
extensionLanding.installSubtitle: Free, no account, no API token
extensionLanding.step1: Install OctoCounts from the Chrome Web Store, Microsoft Edge Add-ons, or Firefox Add-ons — one click, no account.
extensionLanding.step2: Open any public GitHub repository page in your browser.
extensionLanding.step3: The SLOC card appears in the repository sidebar automatically. Click it to open the full panel with the per-language line breakdown.
extensionLanding.permissions: The extension reads the public GitHub repository page you are viewing to detect the owner and repository name, and runs the count against public data through the OctoCounts API. It does not request GitHub account access, needs no API token, works on public repositories only, and collects no personal data. Results are cached locally and by repository and ref so repeat visits load instantly.
extensionLanding.scope: Public GitHub repositories. Private repositories and source-code uploads are not supported; to count private code, run tokei locally.
